diagrams.name: emb-p196-membrane-transport
diagrams.title: Movement of molecules across the cell membrane

cloze.text: A {{c1::reversal line}} is a line formed during {{c2::remodeling}} of cementum, often seen with {{c3::orthodontic tooth movement}}.
{{c1::Hypercementosis}} is thickening of the cementum around the roots, often associated with {{c2::trauma and infection}}.
The {{c1::dental sac}} (the area surrounding the enamel organ) forms the {{c2::cementum, periodontal ligament (PDL), and alveolar bone}}.
The {{c1::periodontal ligament (PDL)}} is the structure that attaches the teeth to the bone.
{{c1::Sharpey's fibers}} are the parts of the PDL fibers embedded in {{c2::bone and cementum}}.
The periodontal ligaments are constantly being {{c1::remodeled}} as they carry {{c2::blood vessels and nerves}}.
Alveolar bone {{c1::supports the teeth}} and is dependent on the {{c2::presence of teeth}}.
If teeth do not erupt, alveolar bone does {{c1::not develop}}; if teeth are lost, the bone {{c2::resorbs}}.
{{c1::Cortical bone}} is compact, dense alveolar bone on the {{c2::buccal and lingual}} sides.
{{c1::Cancellous (spongy)}} bone is {{c2::porous}} bone located between the cortical plates, on the "inside."
The {{c1::cribriform plate}} (alveolar bone proper) is the part of the alveolar bone directly facing the root of the tooth; it contains {{c2::holes}} where blood vessels and nerves penetrate.
Radiographically, the cribriform plate (alveolar bone proper) is called the {{c1::lamina dura}}.
The {{c1::permanent molars}} are non-succedaneous; all other permanent teeth (incisors, canines, premolars) are succedaneous.
Succedaneous teeth erupt in a {{c1::lingual}} position to the primary tooth, except the {{c2::permanent maxillary incisors}}.
Because non-succedaneous teeth do not replace a primary tooth, their eruption position is {{c1::independent of one}}.
{{c1::Nasmyth's membrane}} is a thin layer of tissue residue from eruption, present on both succedaneous and non-succedaneous teeth, that can leave a removable {{c2::green extrinsic}} stain.
The oral cavity is lined by {{c1::stratified squamous}} epithelium.
The oral epithelium acts as a {{c1::protective}} barrier that can be renewed by {{c2::mitosis}}.
The oral epithelium is composed of epithelium, {{c1::basement membrane}}, {{c2::connective tissue}}, and, in some cases, {{c3::submucosa}}.
{{c1::Connective tissue}} fills the space between the tissues and organs of the body; it includes loose connective tissue, cartilage, bone marrow, alveolar bone, and dental tissues.
All dental tissues (cementum, dentin, pulp) are specialized connective tissues except {{c1::enamel}}, which is an {{c2::epithelial}} tissue.
The interface between epithelium and connective tissue is the {{c1::basement membrane}}.
{{c1::Rete pegs}} are inward projections of epithelium into the connective tissue that increase the {{c2::surface area}} of the two tissues and strengthen the connection.
The {{c1::stippling}} of the attached gingiva is caused by {{c2::rete pegs}}.
Rete pegs are NOT present on {{c1::sulcular or junctional}} epithelium.
The connective tissue underlying the oral epithelium is the {{c1::lamina propria}}; it contains salivary glands, sebaceous glands, blood, nerves, collagen, and elastin.
The {{c1::reticular}} layer of the lamina propria is a netlike arrangement of collagen fibers; the {{c2::papillary}} layer is composed of thin, loose collagen fibers.
The {{c1::submucosa}} is loose connective tissue present only in areas needing extra {{c2::cushion and flexibility}} (e.g., cheeks).
{{c1::Lining}} mucosa acts as a barrier between the oral cavity and the deeper structures.
Lining mucosa is soft, moist, cushiony, elastic, and {{c1::non-keratinized}}.
{{c1::Masticatory}} mucosa is present on areas closely related to chewing; it is firm, resilient, has {{c2::more rete pegs}}, and is {{c3::keratinized}}.
The {{c1::ventral}} side of the tongue is covered by lining mucosa; the {{c2::dorsal}} side by masticatory mucosa.
The {{c1::soft}} palate is covered by lining mucosa; the {{c2::hard}} palate by masticatory mucosa.
The surface of the tongue is covered by various types of {{c1::papillae}}, some of which house {{c2::taste buds}}.
{{c1::Filiform}} papillae are the most numerous, covering the {{c2::anterior 2/3}} of the dorsal tongue.
{{c1::Filiform}} papillae are the only papillae with {{c2::no}} taste buds.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Filiform has NO taste feelings; they are here to just "fill" the space.

cloze.text: Elongation of filiform papillae can cause {{c1::black hairy tongue}}; filiform papillae are lost in {{c2::rhomboid glossitis}}.
{{c1::Fungiform}} papillae are {{c2::mushroom}}-shaped on the dorsal tongue and noticeably red from rich vascularization.
{{c1::Circumvallate}} papillae are large, dome-shaped, in a {{c2::V-shaped row}} on the posterior dorsal surface, in front of the sulcus terminalis and foramen cecum.
{{c1::Von Ebner's}} salivary glands empty a {{c2::serous}} secretion to flush the circumvallate papillae.
{{c1::Foliate}} papillae are elongated papillae on the {{c2::side}} of the tongue (they have taste buds).
{{c1::Keratin}} is a fibrous protein with {{c2::no nuclei}} that makes tissue {{c3::stiffer and waterproof}}.
Keratin is found in the {{c1::superficial}} layer of the epithelium.
The most heavily keratinized tissues of the body are the {{c1::palms of the hands and soles of the feet}}.
Keratinized oral mucosa is tightly bound to the {{c1::hard palate and gingiva}}.
Keratinized mucosa supports underlying tissues by resisting the {{c1::loading forces exerted during mastication}}.
Lining mucosa in the cheeks, lips, and floor of the mouth is {{c1::mobile}} to create space when chewing and talking.
Non-keratinized cells {{c1::have nuclei}} and cover the more {{c2::flexible}} areas, such as the mucosal lining of the cheeks.
{{c1::Melanocytes}} are cells in the {{c2::basal}} layer of the epithelium that produce pigmentation.
In the oral cavity, benign pigmentation occurs on the {{c1::attached gingiva}}.
Human organs are made of {{c1::tissues}}, which are composed of {{c2::cells}}.
Human and fungal cells are {{c1::eukaryotes}}; bacteria are {{c2::prokaryotes}}.
{{c1::Prokaryotes}} are very small cells without an organized {{c2::nucleus}} — their DNA floats in the cell.
The {{c1::cell membrane}} is a protein and lipid layer that protects the cell.
The {{c1::cytoplasm}} is the aqueous substance that holds the organelles within the cell.
The {{c1::nucleus}} contains DNA and stores the cell's genetic code.
The {{c1::endoplasmic reticulum}} is a network of membranes and spaces within the cell.
The {{c1::Golgi complex}} is a stack of sacs that {{c2::packages and distributes proteins}} out of the cell; it also synthesizes {{c3::lysosomes}}.
{{c1::Lysosomes}} (made by the Golgi complex) break down foreign substances.
The {{c1::mitochondria}} are the "powerhouse" of the cell, generating {{c2::ATP}} as the cell's energy source.
{{c1::Mitosis}} is nuclear division in {{c2::somatic}} cells (the cells that make up the body).
A {{c1::diploid}} cell contains two sets of chromosomes, one inherited from each parent.
{{c1::Meiosis}} is a modified cell division in {{c2::gamete (sex)}} cells, with {{c3::two}} rounds of cell division but only {{c4::one}} round of DNA replication.
A {{c1::haploid}} cell contains only one set of chromosomes.
{{c1::Junctional}} epithelium attaches the gingiva to the tooth surface by {{c2::hemidesmosomes}}.
{{c1::Diffusion}} is movement of molecules from {{c2::high to low}} concentration; no energy is needed.
{{c1::Facilitated diffusion}} (passive transport) is movement of water-soluble molecules with the help of a {{c2::carrier protein}}; no energy is needed.
{{c1::Active transport}} requires {{c2::energy (ATP)}} and proteins to force molecules into and out of the cell.
{{c1::Osmosis}} is movement of {{c2::water}} molecules across a semipermeable membrane from an area of {{c3::lower}} solute concentration to an area of higher solute concentration.
cloze.extra: Purpose: to balance solute levels on both sides. Lower solute = more water.

mcq.question: On a periapical radiograph, the thin radiopaque line outlining the tooth socket is the lamina dura. Anatomically, this structure is the:
options: C. Cortical plate on the buccal side
mcq.explanation: The cribriform plate — the alveolar bone proper facing the root, perforated by vessels and nerves — is called the lamina dura radiographically. Cortical plates are the outer buccal/lingual bone; the PDL is soft tissue (radiolucent space).

mcq.question: Each of the following dental tissues is a specialized connective tissue EXCEPT one. Which is the exception?
mcq.explanation: Enamel is an epithelial tissue; cementum, dentin, and pulp are specialized connective tissues.

mcq.question: The orange-peel stippling of healthy attached gingiva is produced by which structure?
mcq.explanation: Rete pegs (epithelial projections into connective tissue) cause stippling. Attached gingiva has no submucosa (submucosa is only where cushion is needed, e.g., cheeks).

mcq.question: A patient presents with an elongated, dark, hair-like coating on the dorsum of the tongue (black hairy tongue). Which papillae are elongated?
mcq.explanation: Elongation of filiform papillae (the most numerous, anterior 2/3 of the dorsum) causes black hairy tongue. Fungiform papillae are mushroom-shaped and red, not elongated.

mcq.question: A biopsy taken from which site would show NON-keratinized epithelium?
mcq.explanation: The ventral tongue is lining mucosa (non-keratinized). Hard palate, attached gingiva, and dorsal tongue are masticatory mucosa (keratinized).

mcq.question: Benign physiologic pigmentation of the attached gingiva is produced by which cells?
options: B. Melanocytes in the basal layer
D. Keratinocytes in the stratum corneum
mcq.answer: B. Melanocytes in the basal layer
mcq.explanation: Melanocytes, located in the basal layer, produce pigmentation (melanin). Langerhans and Merkel cells are other cells in the epithelium but do not produce pigment.

mcq.question: The junctional epithelium attaches the gingiva to the tooth surface by means of:
mcq.explanation: Hemidesmosomes attach a cell to a non-cellular surface (the tooth). Desmosomes attach neighboring cells to each other.

mcq.question: Water moves across a semipermeable membrane from an area of low solute concentration to an area of high solute concentration. This process is:
mcq.explanation: Osmosis is movement of water toward the higher solute concentration to balance solute levels. Diffusion moves molecules (solutes) from high to low concentration.

mcq.question: Hard tooth surfaces, including enamel and dentin, develop during which stage of tooth formation?
mcq.explanation: During the maturation stage, dental tissues develop into their mature forms and undergo calcification by the deposition of hydroxyapatite crystals, forming the hard tooth surfaces.

mcq.question: The enamel organ, dental papilla and dental follicle collectively form one unit referred to as the:
mcq.explanation: The tooth germ is the embryonic structure that develops into a tooth, consisting of the enamel organ, dental papilla, and dental sac (follicle).

mcq.question: Which is a correct statement?
options: A. In the oral cavity, the midsagittal plane is called the midline, or median line-of-separation
B. The permanent premolars are considered non-succedaneous
C. In the universal naming system, the mandibular left second molar is number 31
D. The first teeth to erupt in the oral cavity are usually the deciduous maxillary central incisors
mcq.answer: A. In the oral cavity, the midsagittal plane is called the midline, or median line-of-separation
mcq.explanation: The midsagittal plane divides the oral cavity into equal right and left halves and is referred to as the midline or median line-of-separation.

mcq.question: Which epithelial tissue surrounding the tooth is nonkeratinized?
options: A. Inner surface of the free gingival margin
B. Outer surface of the free gingiva
mcq.answer: A. Inner surface of the free gingival margin
mcq.explanation: The sulcular epithelium (the inner surface of the free gingival margin) and the junctional epithelium are nonkeratinized.

mcq.question: Endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm are the three primary layers formed early in embryonic development. The ectoderm layer differentiates into each of the following EXCEPT one. Which one is the exception?
mcq.explanation: The ectoderm gives rise to the skin, nervous system (brain), hair, and nails. The circulatory system primarily develops from the mesoderm. (The book's 5th option, "E. Hair" — also ectoderm — is omitted to fit the 4-option format.)

mcq.question: Red blood cells, most white blood cells, and platelets are produced in the:
mcq.explanation: Hematopoiesis, the process of forming blood cellular components, occurs primarily in the red bone marrow.

mcq.question: During embryonic development the primitive mouth is called the:
mcq.explanation: The stomodeum is the embryonic invagination that develops into the oral cavity. (The book's 5th option, "E. Mandibular pharyngeal arch", is omitted to fit the 4-option format.)

mcq.question: The type of epithelial tissue that is found in the oral cavity is called:
mcq.explanation: The oral cavity is primarily lined with stratified squamous epithelium, which provides protection against abrasion.

mcq.question: Which embryonic structure gives rise to the enamel of teeth?
mcq.explanation: Inner enamel epithelium cells differentiate into ameloblasts, which are responsible for enamel formation.

mcq.question: Which is derived from the first pharyngeal (branchial) arch?
mcq.explanation: The first arch gives rise to the maxillary and mandibular processes, forming much of the face and jaw.

mcq.question: What is the origin of the cementum of the tooth?
mcq.explanation: This ectomesenchymal tissue forms the cementum, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone — the supporting structures of the tooth.

mcq.question: Which germ layer gives rise to the oral epithelium?
mcq.explanation: The oral epithelium, which gives rise to structures like the enamel organ, originates from surface ectoderm.

mcq.question: Which event marks the beginning of the bell stage in tooth development?
options: A. Formation of the dental lamina
D. Differentiation of enamel organ layers
mcq.answer: D. Differentiation of enamel organ layers
mcq.explanation: The bell stage is characterized by the distinct layering of the enamel organ: outer enamel epithelium, stellate reticulum, stratum intermedium, and inner enamel epithelium.

mcq.question: Which is a characteristic of masticatory mucosa?
options: A. Non-keratinized epithelium covering the inner cheeks
B. Found on the hard palate and attached gingiva
D. Lines the floor of the mouth and vestibule
mcq.answer: B. Found on the hard palate and attached gingiva
mcq.explanation: Masticatory mucosa is keratinized and located in areas subject to friction and pressure, such as the hard palate and attached gingiva.

mcq.question: What is the primary function of rete pegs in oral epithelium?
options: A. Secrete collagen fibers into the lamina propria
B. Provide vascular supply to keratinized tissues
C. Increase surface area for epithelial-connective tissue attachment
D. House sensory nerve endings for taste and pressure
mcq.answer: C. Increase surface area for epithelial-connective tissue attachment
mcq.explanation: Rete pegs (rete ridges) are extensions of epithelium into the connective tissue that help anchor the tissue and resist shear forces, especially in areas like masticatory mucosa.
